title: Allowable Complex Black Holes in the Euclidean Gravitational Path Integral
text:
Motivation and setup
The gravitational path integral provides a way to calculate black-hole thermodynamics by summing over spacetime geometries. Its practical successes raise a difficult question: which geometries belong in that sum? Supersymmetric black holes make the question particularly sharp. The Euclidean solutions used to compute their protected partition function have complex metrics. Requiring an ordinary real, positive-definite geometry would discard precisely the saddle points needed for the calculation.
The starting point is the Euclidean gravitational path integral:
\[
\mathcal{Z}=\int\mathcal{D}g_{\mu\nu}\mathcal{D}\Psi\,e^{-I_{E}[g_{\mu\nu},\Psi]}~,
\]
Here \(g_{\mu\nu}\) describes geometry, \(\Psi\) denotes the remaining fields, and \(I_E\) is their Euclidean action. Boundary conditions specify the observable being computed. In a semiclassical treatment, this formal integral is approximated by contributions from saddle points. Finding a solution of the equations of motion, however, does not by itself establish that the solution is an admissible contribution.
This work tests a proposed admissibility rule against an independent boundary-theory calculation. The setting is type IIB string theory on asymptotically \(AdS_5\times S^5\), dual to \(\mathcal{N}=4\) supersymmetric Yang–Mills theory. The analysis allows two unequal angular momenta while restricting the three electric charges to be equal. The observable is the superconformal index, a protected trace whose non-supersymmetric contributions cancel. Its convergence can be constrained directly from the spectrum of the boundary theory.
In particular, supersymmetric derivatives generate arbitrarily large angular momentum. Their contributions must be suppressed, requiring the renormalized angular chemical potentials to have positive real parts:
\[
\operatorname{Re}(\Omega_{a,b}^{\prime})>0\,.
\]
There are additional positivity conditions on the regulator and electric chemical potentials. Together they define the region where the index has its statistical interpretation. The gravitational question is whether the geometry itself recognizes these boundaries.

title: Allowable Complex Black Holes in the Euclidean Gravitational Path Integral
text:
Construction and results
The test uses the Kontsevich–Segal–Witten, or KSW, criterion. It asks whether auxiliary real matter fields have appropriately convergent kinetic terms on a complex background. For every real, nonzero \(p\)-form \(F\), the pointwise requirement is
\[
\mathrm{Re}\left(\sqrt{\det g}\,g^{i_{1}j_{1}}\ldots g^{i_{p}j_{p}}F_{i_{1}\ldots i_{p}}F_{j_{1}\ldots j_{p}}\right)>0~,
\]
This condition ranges over the allowed form degrees, including the scalar case. It is a local test throughout spacetime rather than a comparison of the total actions of different black holes. For a diagonal form of the complex metric, it has the equivalent expression
\[
\sum_{i}|\arg\lambda_{i}|<\pi~.
\]
The \(\lambda_i\) are the diagonal metric entries after the appropriate change of basis. The complex symmetric metric transforms by congruence, so the relevant diagonalization differs from that of a Hermitian matrix. A practical procedure separates the determinant-weighted metric into real symmetric matrices. Positivity of its real part allows a simultaneous reduction using a generalized eigenvalue problem, yielding the phases that enter the criterion.
The black-hole solutions are analytically continued to finite-temperature complex Euclidean saddles with supersymmetric boundary conditions. The analysis begins near the asymptotic boundary, where the expressions simplify. The scalar condition reproduces positivity of the real part of the inverse temperature. The one-form condition yields the angular-potential inequalities already required by convergence of the index. At the angular poles, the higher-form tests do not impose additional restrictions beyond the lower-form conditions.



Figure 1. Parameter-space cross sections \((a,r_+)\) at \(r_*=0.1\). Green marks the region satisfying the \(p=1\) KSW condition near the asymptotic \(AdS_5\) boundary. From left to right, \(\vartheta=0,\pi/4,\pi/2\). The condition holds for every angle inside the red curves, which bound the convergence region of the superconformal index. (arXiv:2602.05979)


The full geometry requires more than an asymptotic test. Numerical checks examine finite radii and several polar angles, applying the scalar, one-form, and higher-form conditions sequentially. In these scans the strongest restrictions arise at the asymptotic boundary and the two angular poles. The higher-form conditions introduce no stronger boundary in the tested bulk region. The resulting allowed set agrees with the convergence region identified independently in the field theory.

title: Allowable Complex Black Holes in the Euclidean Gravitational Path Integral
text:
Bulk geometry and grey galaxies



Figure 2. Parameter-space cross sections \((a,r_+)\) at \(r_*=0.1\). Green marks saddles satisfying all KSW conditions; red curves bound index convergence. Columns have \(\vartheta=0,\pi/4,\pi/2\), and rows have \(r=0.5,2,4,\infty\). The strongest constraints occur at infinity and at the two angular poles. (arXiv:2602.05979)


The location of the failure carries physical information. It occurs far from the black-hole core and is associated with one angular-momentum component. That pattern is consistent with a grey galaxy: a central black hole accompanied by a distant, dilute gas carrying a macroscopic share of the angular momentum. The standard single-center saddle ceases to be an adequate description in precisely the region where a two-component phase is expected to matter.
The correspondence between the gravitational and statistical conditions can be understood through the charges of the gas. A tower of supersymmetric derivatives raises one angular momentum while preserving the BPS condition. As the real part of its conjugate potential approaches zero, large-angular-momentum states cease to be exponentially suppressed. In the bulk, these excitations can sit at large radius, carrying substantial angular momentum with a relatively small effect on the core. The asymptotic location and angular dependence of the KSW failure therefore agree with the expected spatial structure of this instability.
In the equal-electric-charge sector considered here, the analytic asymptotic calculation and numerical radial checks identify the same physical boundary. Positivity of certain factors in the angular-potential inequalities is checked computationally across parameter space, and the finite-radius scans support the conclusion that the boundary test is the strongest one. This agreement connects a local positivity requirement on complex geometry to the convergence of a protected quantum-state count.
The two-component interpretation also organizes the thermodynamics. A black-hole core retains the macroscopic entropy, while a dilute BPS gas stores the excess angular momentum. The expected equilibrium configuration has chemical potentials within the convergent region of the index. In this way, admissibility of the Euclidean saddle and redistribution of charges in the Lorentzian description provide complementary views of the same change of phase.

title: Supersymmetric Grey Galaxies, Dual Dressed Black Holes and the Superconformal Index
text:
Motivation and setup
Black-hole entropy is a count of microscopic states, but identifying exactly which states are counted can be subtle. In strongly coupled \(\mathcal{N}=4\) Yang–Mills theory, known supersymmetric black holes occupy a four-dimensional sheet inside a five-dimensional space of conserved charges. It might seem that exponentially many supersymmetric states exist only near this sheet. This paper proposes a broader picture: a black hole can share charge with supersymmetric excitations outside its horizon, producing large entropy away from the single-black-hole locus.
The five charges are three electric or R-charges \(Q_1,Q_2,Q_3\) and two angular momenta \(J_1,J_2\). Their gravitational setting is type IIB theory on \(AdS_5\times S^5\). The analysis concerns the leading large-\(N\) entropy, with charges of order \(N^2\). It uses known black-hole thermodynamics and motivated conjectures to predict where different kinds of supersymmetric states dominate.
The paper distinguishes an ordinary degeneracy from the superconformal index. A degeneracy counts states at definite charges. The index instead makes a signed count that combines states along lines in charge space. The direction of these lines is
\[
t_{I}=\frac{1}{2}\left(1,1,1,-1,-1\right).
\]
Moving along this direction increases the three electric charges while reducing the two angular momenta, without changing the charge combinations resolved by the index. Consequently, an index coefficient cannot automatically be interpreted as the number of states at one particular point. Even where an index line intersects the black hole sheet, other points along it may contain more states.
This observation motivates the two separate questions addressed in the paper: what is the entropy at specified values of all five charges, and which contribution survives as the leading term after taking the signed sum along an index line? The proposed answers rely on different conjectures and carry different levels of evidence.

title: Supersymmetric Grey Galaxies, Dual Dressed Black Holes and the Superconformal Index
text:
Construction and results
The first ingredient is a black hole dressed by supersymmetric excitations. Grey galaxies place angular momentum in a distant gas of high-spin gravitons. Dual dressed black holes place electric charge in dual giant gravitons. Revolving black holes, related to supersymmetric descendants, can share the leading thermodynamics of grey galaxies. The gas or dressing carries a substantial fraction of the charge, while the black-hole core supplies the leading entropy.
The charges split as
\[
Z_{i}=Z_{i}^{BH}+Z_{i}^{gas},
\]
Here \(Z_i\) denotes the five charges collectively. The core charges lie on the black hole sheet, while the macroscopic gas charges are nonnegative. At leading order, the proposed components can be treated as noninteracting for the purpose of adding charges and evaluating entropy. The dressed concentration conjecture then prescribes the maximization
\[
\max_{Z_{i}^{\prime}}S_{BH}(Z_{i}^{\prime}),~~~(Z_{i}^{\prime}\leq Z_{i}~~~\forall i=1\ldots 5)
\]
The optimization ranges over allowed black-hole cores. Rather than restricting large entropy to a thin sheet, it extends that entropy into the surrounding charge space. An algorithm identifies the optimal core and which charge components reside in the dressing. The resulting microcanonical ground-state diagram has eleven phases: the pure black-hole phase, three grey-galaxy phases, and seven dual-dressed phases.



Figure 1. A \(\mathbb B^3\) slice of the black hole sheet. Blue equal-charge planes separate the cores of the three rank-two dual-dressed phases; their surfaces seed the rank-four phases and their intersection seeds the rank-six phase. The red equal-angular-momentum plane separates the two rank-two grey-galaxy cores and seeds the rank-four grey-galaxy phase. (arXiv:2501.17217)


The rank labels count the independent rotation planes occupied by the dressing. A rank-two dual dressed phase carries one electric-charge component outside the core; rank four carries two; rank six carries three. Equal-charge surfaces determine where these possibilities meet. Similarly, grey galaxies distinguish dressing in one or both angular-momentum planes. These are different outcomes of the same constrained entropy problem, rather than separate assumptions about unrelated solutions.
The known core black holes satisfy a nonlinear density relation, with lowercase charges normalized by \(N^2\):
\[
\displaystyle\frac{j_{1}j_{2}}{2}+q_{1}q_{2}q_{3}=\left(q_{1}+q_{2}+q_{3}+\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(q_{1}q_{2}+q_{1}q_{3}+q_{2}q_{3}-\frac{1}{2}(j_{1}+j_{2})\right),
\]
The second ingredient, the unobstructed saddle conjecture, addresses the index. It assumes that the alternating signs do not suppress the leading exponential contribution selected by the largest supersymmetric entropy along an index line. Combining this assumption with the first maximization predicts nine index phases. One is dominated by the ordinary intersection black hole; the other eight are dominated by grey-galaxy or dual-dressed configurations. Thus agreement between the index and the intersection black hole is expected only in part of charge space.

title: Supersymmetric Grey Galaxies, Dual Dressed Black Holes and the Superconformal Index
text:
Microscopic evidence and index phases



Figure 2. Numerical indicial entropy \(N^{-2}\log|n_I|\) at \(N=10\), with \(2(Z_1+Z_2+Z_3)+3(Z_4+Z_5)=90\), as a function of \(j_R=(Z_4-Z_5)/N^2\). Red dots are numerical data. Blue curves give the intersection-black-hole entropy and orange gives the grey-galaxy entropy; the combined solid curve is the prediction under the unobstructed saddle conjecture. (arXiv:2501.17217)


The field-theory index supplies an independent comparison at \(N\leq10\). On the charge slice shown above, the numerical data follow the pure-black-hole curve near the central region and then track the grey-galaxy prediction as the angular-momentum imbalance grows. The transition changes which core supplies the leading entropy. It is visible even at these moderate ranks because the selected slice separates the two predictions and keeps the graviton contribution relatively small in the discriminating region.
The two conjectures organize different aspects of this microscopic picture. Supersymmetric descendants give concrete examples of black holes carrying additional angular momentum. Probe dual giants and directly enumerated field-theory states support the possibility of electric-charge dressing. These examples motivate the dressed concentration prescription, which maximizes over the known single-center black-hole family. The more tentative unobstructed saddle assumption then relates that positive degeneracy problem to the signed sum defining the index. Qualitative agreement with finite-\(N\) data provides evidence for the combined prediction on the studied charge slices.
In the grand canonical description, the phase structure has a simple chemical-potential interpretation. In a grey-galaxy phase, the angular-momentum component stored in the dressing is associated with a vanishing renormalized angular potential. In a dual-dressed phase, the corresponding electric potential vanishes. A growing amount of charge can then reside outside the core while the relevant potential remains pinned to its phase boundary. The rank of the dressing records how many independent charge components participate in this redistribution.
This picture explains both the familiar entropy match and its predicted extensions. When the optimal point on an index line is the intersection black hole, the leading index agrees with its area-law entropy. When the optimum moves into a dressed phase, the entropy is instead set by a different core whose remaining charges are supplied by the exterior excitations. The nine-phase index diagram is therefore the projection of a richer eleven-phase ground-state problem, with the index retaining four independent combinations of the five conserved charges.

title: Dual Dressed Black Holes as the End Point of the Charged Superradiant Instability in N = 4 Yang Mills
text:
Motivation and setup
A black hole in anti-de Sitter space can lose stability when it becomes favorable to transfer charge from its horizon to material outside it. The reflecting asymptotic geometry allows emitted excitations to remain in the system. The question is then thermodynamic as well as dynamical: at fixed total energy and charges, what configuration replaces the unstable black hole? This paper investigates that question in type IIB string theory on \(AdS_5\times S^5\), the gravitational dual of strongly coupled \(\mathcal{N}=4\) Yang–Mills theory.
Earlier descriptions emphasized charged scalar condensates and hairy black holes in a five-dimensional gauged-supergravity truncation. The ten-dimensional theory extends this description with an infinite tower of charged excitations, supplying additional channels through which the black hole can redistribute charge. The paper shows that large dual giant gravitons provide an instability channel that is absent from the restricted description. In particular, previously proposed hairy endpoints can themselves discharge into these objects.
A dual giant is a D3-brane expanded into the anti-de Sitter directions while carrying angular momentum on the internal sphere. The proposed endpoint contains a central black hole and one, two, or three very large dual giants. Each giant carries charge of order \(N^2\) and lies at a radial position of order \(\sqrt{N}\) in AdS units. Their large separation makes a weakly interacting composite possible even though the total energy outside the horizon is macroscopic.
The charges, energy, and effective flux of the core are
\[
\begin{split}
&N_{\rm eff}=N-m\\
&E^{BH}=E^{\rm tot}-\sum_{i=1}^{3}Q_i^D\\
&Q_i^{BH}=Q_i^{\rm tot}-Q_i^D\\
&J_i^{BH}=J_i^{\rm tot}.
\end{split}
\]
Here \(m\) is the number of dual giants, \(Q_i^D\) their charges, and \(N_{\rm eff}\) the five-form flux seen by the central black hole. The small flux reduction is important for selecting how many giants occur, even though it is subleading in the leading large-\(N\) thermodynamics.



Figure 1. Fixed-charge paths through the zero-angular-momentum phase diagram of \(\mathcal{N}=4\) Yang–Mills theory. Decreasing energy gives three dressing phases for unequal charges, two when two charges coincide, and one when all three coincide. (arXiv:2409.18178)

title: Dual Dressed Black Holes as the End Point of the Charged Superradiant Instability in N = 4 Yang Mills
text:
Construction and main results
The dominant entropy comes from the core horizon. Its dependence on the remaining energy, charges, angular momenta, and effective flux takes the form
\[
S_{BH}=N_{\rm eff}^{2}\,s_{BH}\left(\frac{E^{BH}}{N_{\rm eff}^{2}},\frac{Q_i^{BH}}{N_{\rm eff}^{2}},\frac{J_j^{BH}}{N_{\rm eff}^{2}}\right).
\]
At fixed total charges, the preferred division between core and dressing maximizes this entropy. The leading derivative takes a particularly transparent form:
\[
\frac{\partial S_{BH}}{\partial Q_i^D}=\beta(\mu_i-1),\qquad Q^{BH}<Q^{\rm tot}.
\]
The inverse temperature is \(\beta\), and \(\mu_i\) is the core chemical potential. If a potential exceeds unity, moving the corresponding charge into a dual giant increases entropy. An interior equilibrium therefore pins that potential to unity. Channels in which no giant is present instead satisfy the appropriate endpoint condition with potential below unity. Depending on how many channels are occupied, the resulting dual dressed black holes have rank two, four, or six.
The next order in the entropy expansion selects the number of giants through the reduction in effective flux seen by the core. Within the proposed family, this favors the smallest number of giants needed to carry the dressing: one, two, or three in the respective phases. The paper analyzes both unequal-charge nonrotating configurations and equal-charge rotating configurations, displaying phase boundaries and competition with rotationally dressed grey galaxies.
The canonical description reaches the same threshold from another direction. A dual giant becomes macroscopically occupied when a chemical potential approaches unity closely enough. The relevant large-\(N\) scaling is
\[
\mu_i=1-\frac{\chi_i}{N^2}.
\]
The paper also studies the quantum mechanics of a giant near the black hole, including potential tunneling into the horizon. The threshold picked by that analysis agrees with the thermodynamic equilibrium condition. Approximate ten-dimensional solutions incorporate the gravitational backreaction of the large giants: their contribution to the asymptotic charges is significant, while the metric perturbation can still be handled linearly in the appropriate large-\(N\) regime.



Figure 2. Equal-charge phase diagram at \(J_1=J_2=2\). The red \(\mu=1\) and black \(\Omega=1\) curves separate the vacuum black-hole region from dual dressed black holes and grey galaxies; the blue line is the BPS bound. The arrow assigns the entropy of a dressed state to its core. (arXiv:2409.18178)

title: Dual Dressed Black Holes as the End Point of the Charged Superradiant Instability in N = 4 Yang Mills
section: Dressed phases and the gravitational description
text:
Dressed phases and the gravitational description
A dual dressed black hole divides the conserved charges between a central horizon and distant D3-branes. The core supplies the leading entropy, while the surrounding giants carry a macroscopic amount of charge at a small entropy cost. At fixed total charges, the equilibrium condition therefore selects a core at the chemical-potential threshold. This provides a direct geometric interpretation of the phase diagram: different regions correspond to different numbers of charge directions in which the core has reached this threshold.
The proposed dominance of these phases is a conjecture based on large-\(N\) thermodynamics and the approximate gravitational construction at strong coupling. The displayed slices describe the regime in which the five-dimensional cores are stable against localization on the internal sphere. In the nonrotating slice, successive transitions can occur as energy decreases at fixed unequal charges. Equalities among the charges combine these transitions, producing the patterns shown in the first figure. In the rotating slice, charged dressing competes with the angular-momentum dressing of grey galaxies.
The large radius of a giant explains how this composite remains tractable. Locally, its gravitational field is weak at large \(N\). At distances where its full energy and charge contribute to the asymptotic fields, the normalizable perturbation has already decayed strongly. Linearized backreaction can consequently capture a substantial change in the boundary charges. Combining this perturbation with the central black-hole geometry yields the approximate ten-dimensional dressed solutions, with corrections controlled by inverse powers of \(N\).
The quantum probe calculation complements this spacetime picture by examining the exchange of a giant with the horizon. Its stability threshold matches the condition obtained by entropy maximization, connecting microscopic brane dynamics to macroscopic equilibrium. Near supersymmetry, a core with nonzero horizon entropy can coexist with supersymmetric dressing. The resulting configurations motivate a microscopic account of how black-hole states and brane degrees of freedom contribute together to the spectrum of the dual gauge theory.

title: Towards a Classification of Holographic Multi-partite Entanglement Measures
text:
Looking beyond one entanglement surface
In holography, ordinary entanglement entropy connects a boundary quantum state to the area of a minimal surface in a gravitational spacetime. That connection is powerful, but it begins with a division into only two parties. A state split among several regions has many additional patterns of correlation. This paper develops a framework for asking which multipartite quantities admit similarly useful geometric descriptions and which can probe the original bulk geometry, rather than requiring a completely new gravitational solution.
The difference between probing and backreacting is already present for two parties. A Rényi entropy at a general replica index requires a geometry with a finite conical defect. Taking the appropriate limit removes that defect and gives a minimal-area quantity in the original spacetime. The paper seeks multipartite analogues of this mechanism, starting from local-unitary invariants of a pure state and organizing them into families that admit a suitable continuation.
A general invariant is built by contracting copies of the wavefunction with conjugate copies. Each party contributes a permutation specifying how its indices are paired. This description supports both classification and counting: disconnected contraction diagrams factorize, while connected diagrams supply the basic building blocks. There are rapidly growing numbers of possibilities, so geometric usefulness provides an extra selection principle. The classification uses local-unitary invariance to organize the boundary observables, while the probe condition selects those with a particularly direct geometric interpretation.
A particularly tractable family comes from independent cyclic permutations assigned to the parties. The replica data are expressed using integer labels, and special families interpolate toward a probe limit. This construction extends the earlier multi-entropy and allows different pieces of the eventual bulk network to carry different weights. It turns the search for one privileged multipartite number into a structured collection of boundary observables.



Figure 1. Boundary regions \(\mathcal{R}_{\mathtt{a}}\) and their bulk chambers \(\mathcal{C}_{\mathtt{a}}\). Neighboring chambers are separated by walls labeled by the relative party permutation. (arXiv:2304.06082)

title: Towards a Classification of Holographic Multi-partite Entanglement Measures
section: The replica construction and its weighted geometric answer
text:
The replica construction and its weighted geometric answer
To compute these quantities in a field theory, copies of a Euclidean path integral are glued according to their permutations. The resulting replicated boundary is filled by a gravitational saddle. The decisive assumption is that its dominant filling preserves the boundary replica symmetry. When it does, the bulk can be quotiented to a simpler geometry containing conical singularities, with each singular segment associated with a boundary-region interface.
The corresponding cosmic-brane contribution is:
\[
\displaystyle{\mathcal{S}}_{\rm br}^{(k)}=\frac{k-1}{4kG_{N}}\int dy^{D-1}\sqrt{h}=\frac{k-1}{4kG_{N}}A
\]
The cone order sets the brane tension, the induced metric measures its worldvolume, and the area factor makes the geometric content explicit. Continuing toward the probe limit sends the backreaction away. A network of weighted minimal surfaces then remains in the unreplicated geometry. Figure 1 shows the boundary regions and the corresponding bulk chambers, whose separating walls form the web.
The area functional is determined by a weighted minimization:
\[
\displaystyle\partial_{n}{\mathcal{S}}_{\rm grav}|_{n=1}=\frac{1}{4G_{N}}{\rm min}_{\cal W}\left\{\sum_{\widetilde{L}_{\sigma_{\mathtt{a}}^{-1}\sigma_{\mathtt{b}}}\in{\mathcal{W}}}\log({\rm lcm}(m_{\mathtt{a}},m_{\mathtt{b}}))A_{{\mathtt{a}},{\mathtt{b}}}\right\}\equiv\frac{1}{4G_{N}}A_{\rm min}^{\cal W}.
\]
Here the weights are logarithms of least common multiples of the integer party labels. They are fixed by the replica construction rather than chosen by hand. Minimization includes the allowed arrangement of the web, not merely the position of one preselected junction. The resulting probe measure has the compact form:
\[
\displaystyle S^{\{m_{\mathtt{a}}\}}=\frac{1}{4G_{N}}A_{\rm min}^{\cal W}.
\]
This is the multipartite geometric prescription: a weighted area divided by the gravitational coupling. In three bulk dimensions, the areas reduce to lengths of geodesic segments. As an explicit example, the equal-label three-party case reduces to a junction problem. For equal labels, the measure becomes:
\[
\displaystyle S^{\{m,m,m\}}=\frac{\log m}{4G_{N}}{\rm min}_{X}\Big(\sum_{i}\ell(P_{i},X))\Big).
\]
The boundary endpoints are fixed while the interior junction is optimized. Unequal labels generalize the competition among the segments. This makes the geometric meaning of the boundary family concrete: changing the observable changes the web’s tensions and therefore which portions of spacetime it probes.
The paper tests the prescription against two-dimensional CFT calculations involving twist-operator correlation functions and semiclassical conformal blocks. The dependence on boundary positions, including the nontrivial cross-ratio dependence, agrees in the cases analyzed. Three-point coefficients of twist operators supply the remaining normalization data, while the bulk junction calculation predicts their contribution to the probe measure. For four and five connected regions, the calculations also test how this constant contribution scales with the number of trivalent vertices.

title: Towards a Classification of Holographic Multi-partite Entanglement Measures
section: Replica geometries and finer bulk partitions
text:
Replica geometries and finer bulk partitions
Different choices of multipartite measure can draw different webs across the same spacetime. Overlaying them partitions a bulk slice more finely than a single bipartite entanglement wedge does. Figure 2 displays this refinement for several probe webs. Regions inaccessible to one boundary party can be subdivided by observables sensitive to several parties together, motivating questions about a more detailed account of bulk locality.



Figure 2. A bulk Cauchy slice divided into finer regions by brane webs corresponding to several multipartite probe measures. (arXiv:2304.06082)


This geometric refinement suggests a connection to quantum error correction. A bulk region in the entanglement shadow can be reconstructed jointly from certain pairs of boundary parties, even when it lies outside the entanglement wedge of each party separately. Multipartite webs subdivide that shadow, distinguishing regions that share the same bipartite reconstruction description. The paper proposes that multipartite analogues of mutual information could help express the corresponding finer reconstruction properties.
The replica geometry can be studied explicitly in low-genus cases. For three parties at replica index three, the replicated boundary is a torus at a symmetric point in moduli space. Several equally short cycles are exchanged by the replica group, and choosing one to contract in the bulk breaks part of the symmetry. For four parties at index two, the replicated boundary is a rectangular torus. Its independent cycles are preserved by the replica action, allowing an explicit replica-symmetric dominant filling. These examples reveal how cycle structure controls the symmetry of the saddle.
The continuation toward the probe limit connects this discrete replica data to continuous geometric tensions. The paper examines the growth conditions associated with uniqueness of analytic continuation and uses generalized GHZ states to illustrate the structure of the boundary problem. In the semiclassical bulk, the continued conical defects become weighted probe surfaces. Together, the permutation classification, replica-symmetric derivation, and CFT checks establish a systematic framework for relating families of multipartite observables to networks within a single gravitational spacetime.

title: Everyday Radio Telescope
text:
Motivation and setup
Radio astronomy offers a way to study astronomical objects beyond visible light, but the equipment can appear inaccessible to an undergraduate laboratory or amateur group. This project develops an affordable experiment from commercially available satellite-television components. Its aim is educational as well as observational: to connect receiving electronics, digitization, calibration, statistical noise, and astronomical interpretation in a working instrument.
The telescope operates near 11.2 GHz. A parabolic dish concentrates incoming radiation onto a low-noise block receiver, or LNB. A satellite finder acts as a square-law detector, producing a signal related to received intensity. An Arduino Uno digitizes the output with a ten-bit analog-to-digital converter at ten samples per second. A set-top box supplies power, and a Python pipeline records and displays the measurements. The instrument measures the total received intensity across its operating band, connecting changes in detector voltage to sources crossing the antenna beam.



Figure 1. Block diagram of the radio-telescope setup. (arXiv:1601.02982)


The Sun supplies a strong first target. Geostationary satellites provide reference signals for calibration, and sky observations away from a target supply the background. Pointing is manual, using predicted altitude and azimuth. For satellite calibration, rotating the LNB aligns its receiving element with the transmitted polarization and maximizes the detected signal. The resulting voltage change provides a direct demonstration of the receiver’s polarization response.
The calibration begins with the Friis transmission relation:
\[
\frac{P_r}{P_t}=G_tG_r\left(\frac{\lambda}{4\pi R}\right)^2.
\]
Here the received and transmitted powers are \(P_r\) and \(P_t\), the antenna gains are \(G_r\) and \(G_t\), \(R\) is the satellite distance, and \(\lambda\) is the observing wavelength. Satellite equivalent isotropically radiated power combines the transmitter power and gain, allowing the received reference power to be estimated from accessible satellite information.

title: Everyday Radio Telescope
text:
Construction and main results
Converting a voltage change into an astronomical measurement requires both the detector calibration and an estimate of the effective collecting area. The receiving gain is related to dish diameter and aperture efficiency by
\[
G_r=\eta_A\left(\frac{\pi d}{\lambda}\right)^2.
\]
The aperture efficiency \(\eta_A\) accounts for the difference between geometric dish area and effective collecting area. The calibration uses this information to turn the measured satellite voltage above background into a power scale. The solar signal is then calibrated relative to the satellite observation, preferably taken close in time so that instrumental conditions are comparable.
A drift scan holds the antenna pointing fixed while the sky moves through its beam. Fitting the solar transit with a Gaussian provides a beam-width estimate as well as a recognizable source detection. The paper reports beam widths of approximately \(3.4\)–\(3.5\) degrees, with the tabulated fits giving \(3.357\pm0.021\) and \(3.501\pm0.007\) degrees. These measurements agree with the approximate beam width expected for the instrument. The broad beam makes source acquisition forgiving, while also limiting angular resolution.



Figure 2. Drift scan of the Sun. Cyan points show the data, and the black line is a Gaussian fit. (arXiv:1601.02982)


The received power is then converted to flux density, including the single-polarization response and the difference between the satellite’s transmitted bandwidth and the receiver’s solar-observation bandwidth. Dividing the flux by the solar solid angle gives intensity. Assuming thermal radiation in the Rayleigh–Jeans regime, the corresponding brightness temperature is
\[
T=\frac{I\lambda^2}{2K_B}=10078\,K.
\]
Here \(I\) is the inferred intensity, \(K_B\) is Boltzmann’s constant, and the numerical value follows from the measured solar signal in the worked calibration. The two reported solar brightness temperatures are 10078 K and 10136 K, with quoted uncertainties of 295 K and 324 K. Brightness temperature expresses the observed radio intensity as the temperature of a thermal emitter at the operating frequency, characterizing the Sun’s microwave emission.
Sensitivity can improve by averaging longer. The radiometer equation gives the dependence on averaging time and bandwidth:
\[
\sigma_T\propto\frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau\Delta\nu_{RF}}}.
\]
The output fluctuation \(\sigma_T\) decreases as integration time \(\tau\) or receiver bandwidth \(\Delta\nu_{RF}\) increases, under the assumptions behind that noise model. Increasing integration from one second to sixty seconds enabled the reported drift-scan detections of Saturn and a Galactic-arm crossing. The Saturn detection has a reported signal-to-noise ratio of three, with transit timing checked against the predicted sky motion.

title: Everyday Radio Telescope
section: Noise, calibration, and an undergraduate experiment
text:
Noise, calibration, and an undergraduate experiment
The instrument connects several normally separate classroom topics in one measurement. The receiving chain illustrates amplification and detection; the digitizer turns a continuous voltage into a sampled series; calibration connects the output to physical units; and drift scans relate time-domain structure to the motion of the sky. Strong satellite signals make it practical to explore alignment, polarization, and gain before turning to astronomical targets. The Sun then supplies a bright extended source whose transit measures the antenna response.
Characterizing noise is part of this experimental chain. Comparing ordinary sky measurements with measurements taken while the LNB is shielded identifies features generated within the receiving system. Fourier analysis shows a feature around half a hertz that appears in both sets of measurements. This common structure helps connect the measured time series to the electronics and separates different contributions to the output fluctuations.
The surrounding temperature also tracks the detector voltage, with a reported correlation coefficient of 0.98. Measuring that dependence provides a practical introduction to instrumental drift and explains the value of satellite calibration close in time to a solar scan. The temperature conversion combines an assumed aperture efficiency, satellite reference powers, the measured voltage above background, and a bandwidth correction appropriate to broadband solar emission. Each step gives a physical meaning to a quantity that begins as a detector reading.
For weaker sources, the broad receiver bandwidth and longer integration supply the sensitivity gain described by the radiometer relation. The reported Saturn signal, with a signal-to-noise ratio of three, and the Galactic-arm crossing are identified by comparing the measured transit times with the predicted field of view. This ties the observing geometry to the statistical interpretation of the data and makes background measurements central to source identification.
The resulting experiment offers a compact route from commercially available receiving hardware to a calibrated view of the radio sky. It supports exercises in beam-width measurement, flux calibration, thermal-radiation analysis, time-series statistics, and observational planning. Changes in integration time and pointing let students test how the instrument responds, while the acquisition and visualization pipeline makes the connection between hardware settings and measured signals immediately accessible.

section: Flaring in the Permian: What Satellites See vs What Operators Report
text:
Flaring in the Permian: What Satellites See vs What Operators Report
Summer 2026 · Erdős Institute · Team project
Texas operators report vented and flared gas volumes to the Railroad Commission of Texas, but the figures arrive with a delay and remain subject to revision. Satellites observe the heat emitted by the same flares independently of those filings. We asked whether this signal could estimate current flaring before the official figures became available, and whether it could also help predict oil production.

Project repository ↗ Executive summary ↗ Presentation ↗


Building a matched dataset
We combined VIIRS Nightfire satellite observations from the Earth Observation Group with Texas regulatory production and gas-disposition records. Preparing a common dataset required several steps:

Aggregate satellite radiant heat to monthly observations and normalize by the number of clear satellite observations, with a mask for the August 2022 satellite outage.
Join lease-level production records to well identifiers and geographic coordinates. Allocate each lease’s reported volumes uniformly across its wells, making the allocation assumption explicit.
Assign wells to the satellite flare-site footprints containing them, then assemble a panel of matched site and month observations.

This matching step matters because satellite flare-site footprints cover only part of the basin’s production. It defines the sample on which the satellite and regulatory signals can be compared.


Estimating flared gas before the official release
An ARIMAX(1,1,1) model combines the recent history of reported flaring with satellite radiant heat as an additional predictor. We evaluated both a current-month nowcast using that month’s satellite observations and a one-month-ahead forecast. In a 92-month walk-forward backtest, each prediction used the preceding training window, followed by a monthly update of the model.

56.5% → 68.5% directional accuracy
Adding the satellite signal improved the model’s ability to predict whether flaring would rise or fall by 12 percentage points, compared with ARIMA without satellite data, over January 2018–August 2025. The evaluation used final revised regulatory volumes.




Figure 1. Reported vented and flared gas volumes (black) are compared with predictions from ARIMAX using satellite data (red), ARIMA without satellite data (blue), ordinary least squares regression (orange), and the previous month’s volume (grey). Shaded bands show the ARIMA and ARIMAX 95% intervals. Gas volume is measured in thousands of cubic feet (MCF). (Project)


The comparison also shows why the temporal structure matters. Ordinary least squares captures much of the direction of change but has substantially larger absolute errors. Combining the satellite measurement with an autoregressive component helps anchor the predicted level to the system’s recent behavior. XGBoost provided another comparison, with weaker performance during the largest surges.


Why flaring does not provide a stable oil-production proxy
The proposed path to oil production passed through several physical relationships: satellite heat measures flaring, flaring is a fraction of casinghead gas, and gas production is related to oil production. The latter relationships changed over the study period. As new pipelines became available around 2019–2020, the flared fraction fell to roughly 2%, while the gas-to-oil ratio more than doubled.



Figure 2. Monthly oil production (blue, left axis, in barrels) and satellite radiant heat (red, right axis) rise together before 2019, then follow different paths. The two vertical axes have different units. Their changing relationship explains why a model calibrated during the early growth period does not provide a stable oil-production estimate later. (Project)


Oil forecasts therefore showed little consistent improvement over models using oil’s own history. The useful satellite signal is an early estimate of flaring itself. That distinction helps identify where satellite monitoring can inform infrastructure planning and environmental monitoring without treating a changing flaring-to-production relationship as a fixed conversion.
Team: Abhishek Koparde, Amey Joshi, Sabarenath Jayaprakash, and Vineeth Krishna Talasila.

title: Research
text:
Quantum Information in Quantum Gravity

From two subsystems to many
Entanglement entropy measures quantum correlations across a division into two parts. In a pure state with three or more subsystems, there are additional ways for correlations to be shared. Grouping parties together can hide this structure: the entropies of individual subsystems need not capture every invariant of the full state. My work develops measures that treat the multiple parties together and asks how their algebraic structure appears in gravity.
The starting point is the replica method. For a bipartite system, copies of a reduced density matrix are joined cyclically, and the resulting contraction gives a Rényi entropy. The multi-entropy construction instead uses a lattice of replicas, with a separate cyclic permutation associated with each party. The resulting Rényi multi-entropy is
\[
S^{({\mathtt{q}})}_{n}\equiv\frac{1}{1-n}{\rm Log}\,({\mathcal{Z}}_{n}^{({\mathtt{q}})}/({\mathcal{Z}}_{1}^{({\mathtt{q}})})^{n^{{\mathtt{q}}-1}}).
\]
Here \(\mathtt{q}\) counts the parties, \(n\) is the replica parameter, and \(\mathcal{Z}^{(\mathtt{q})}_n\) is the specified contraction of copies of the state and its conjugate. The normalization removes dependence on the norm of the state. The construction reduces to the familiar Rényi entropy for two parties, while retaining information about more general multipartite correlations.



Figure 1. A three-party state can be represented by a density matrix (left). Joining copies of this matrix in a periodic lattice (right) gives the contraction \(\mathcal{Z}^{(3)}_4\) used to define multi-entropy. The lattice labels replicas of the state. (arXiv:2206.09723)


Continuing the replica parameter toward one defines multi-entropy itself:
\[
S^{({\mathtt{q}})}={\rm lim}_{n\to{1}}\,S^{({\mathtt{q}})}_{n}.
\]
This continuation relates the integer-replica contractions to a continuous entropy-like quantity. A related question is how these quantities change when two parties are merged. Work on the monotonicity conjecture proves particular cases and develops evidence for others, while leaving the general statement conjectural.


Replica symmetry and bulk geometry
In holography, a quantum field theory admits a gravitational description in one higher dimension. Ordinary entanglement entropy is encoded by an extremal area. The multipartite problem suggests a richer structure: networks of surfaces that partition the bulk into chambers, with junctions where surfaces meet. The replica construction determines the gluing of boundary regions; a compatible bulk saddle must implement that gluing geometrically.



Figure 2. Boundary regions \(\mathcal{R}_{\mathtt a}\) are associated with bulk chambers \(\mathcal{C}_{\mathtt a}\). The walls separating neighboring chambers form a network of surfaces, with labels fixed by the replica permutations of the adjacent regions. (arXiv:2304.06082)


The classification program studies more general permutation contractions and the finite groups organizing their replica symmetries. The subsequent bulk replica symmetry analysis asks when those symmetries can extend to a smooth covering geometry. This constrains which proposed networks admit a symmetric gravitational realization. The goal is to identify the quantum observables and the geometric assumptions required for each correspondence, including the possibility that a dominant saddle breaks replica symmetry.

title: Research
text:
Black Holes and Holography

Black holes with charge outside the horizon
In anti-de Sitter space, a black hole can share its conserved charges with matter outside its horizon. I study such configurations in AdS/CFT and determine which phase has the largest entropy at fixed energy, charge, and angular momentum. The resulting phase diagrams describe new equilibrium states of the dual quantum field theory.
A central example is a dual dressed black hole: a black-hole core surrounded by a small number of large dual giant gravitons. These expanded branes carry electric charge, while the core supplies the leading entropy. The charged-superradiance study constructs these configurations in \(AdS_5\times S^5\) and analyzes how they arise when a charged black hole becomes unstable. Entropy maximization determines how the total charge is divided between the core and its dressing.
Grey galaxies provide a rotational counterpart, with angular momentum carried by a distant gas. Together, charged and rotational dressing extend the supersymmetric ground-state phases beyond the family of isolated black holes. In the two-charge \(AdS_4\) analysis, supersymmetric states saturate the energy bound
\[
E\ell\geq J+2(Q_{1}\ell+Q_{2}\ell)~.
\]
Here \(\ell\) is the AdS radius, \(E\) is energy, \(J\) is angular momentum, and \(Q_1,Q_2\) are electric charges. Regular single-center supersymmetric black holes satisfy a further nonlinear charge relation, forming a surface in charge space. Combining a core with an additional gas produces distinct phases on either side of that surface.



Figure 3. Supersymmetric single-center black holes lie on a curved sheet in the space of electric-charge densities and angular momentum. The translucent foreground shows where the sheet folds over into a second branch. Configurations containing a core and a gas extend the phase diagram beyond this sheet. (arXiv:2510.16274)




Phase transitions and the superconformal index
The superconformal index is a protected, signed count of quantum states. Its charge combinations group states along lines in charge space. A new dressed configuration can dominate the leading entropy on such a line, changing the phase predicted for the index. In the grey-galaxy and index study, an entropy-maximization prescription, together with the unobstructed saddle conjecture, predicts nine index phases. The numerical index provides an independent test of those predictions.



Figure 4. Numerical index entropy at \(N=10\) (red points) is compared with the single-black-hole prediction (blue) and the grey-galaxy prediction (orange), as the angular-momentum imbalance \(j_R\) varies at fixed index-charge combination. The combined solid curve follows the black-hole branch before changing to the grey-galaxy branch, matching the trend in the numerical data. (arXiv:2501.17217)


The change from the blue branch to the orange branch is a direct signature of the proposed phase transition. The finite-\(N\) data follow the trend expected from the leading large-\(N\) calculation, showing how configurations with matter outside the horizon change the microscopic count. The distinction between entropy at fixed charges and the signed index is central to this comparison.
I also study the Euclidean gravitational description of these transitions. Supersymmetric black holes contribute complex saddles to the path integral. The complex-black-hole analysis applies the Kontsevich–Segal–Witten criterion to this family and finds that geometric admissibility tracks the convergence region of the boundary index. This supplies a gravitational diagnostic for the onset of grey-galaxy physics.

title: A New Multipartite Entanglement Measure and Its Holographic Dual
text: Skip to main content

title: A New Multipartite Entanglement Measure and Its Holographic Dual
text:
Motivation and setup
Entanglement entropy is a powerful bridge between quantum information and geometry. It describes how a pure quantum state is shared between two subsystems. In a holographic theory, the same quantity can be calculated from a surface in the gravitational bulk. A state shared among three or more parties contains additional structure, however: choosing a single division into two groups can hide distinctions between different patterns of multipartite entanglement. This paper asks whether there is a natural, permutation-symmetric extension of entropy that also has a direct geometric description.
The starting point is a pure state in a tensor product of \(\mathtt{q}\) Hilbert spaces. An entanglement quantity must be unchanged by independent unitary changes of basis in each factor. Such invariants can be built by taking copies of the wavefunction and its conjugate, then contracting their indices. In the two-party case, these contractions reduce to products of traces of powers of a reduced density matrix. For more parties, there are many more possible contractions, so extending the familiar entropy requires a specific choice.
The paper selects a family with a regular replica structure. After eliminating redundant relabelings, there are \(n^{\mathtt{q}-1}\) copies arranged on a \((\mathtt{q}-1)\)-dimensional periodic lattice. Each party has its own prescribed cyclic contraction. Although this representation chooses one party to trace out first, the resulting invariant is symmetric under exchange of the original parties. The normalization is included explicitly, so the definition does not depend on an arbitrary norm of the state.
The resulting Rényi multi-entropy is
\[
S^{(\mathtt{q})}_{n}\equiv\frac{1}{1-n}{\rm Log}\,\left(\mathcal{Z}_{n}^{(\mathtt{q})}/\left(\mathcal{Z}_{1}^{(\mathtt{q})}\right)^{n^{\mathtt{q}-1}}\right).
\]
Here \(\mathcal{Z}_{n}^{(\mathtt{q})}\) denotes the prescribed replica contraction. Taking the continuation to \(n=1\) defines multi-entropy. With two parties this recovers the ordinary von Neumann entropy; with more parties it probes a different contraction pattern.



Figure 1. Graphical notation for the density matrix for \(\mathtt{q}=3\) and the index contraction giving \(\mathcal{Z}_4^{(3)}\). (arXiv:2206.09723)

title: A New Multipartite Entanglement Measure and Its Holographic Dual
text:
Construction and main results
A useful check comes from generalized GHZ states, whose basis labels are shared among all parties. The replica contraction can then be evaluated explicitly because a common index runs through the whole network. The resulting multi-entropy is
\[
S^{(\mathtt{q})}=(1-\mathtt{q})\sum_i |\lambda_i|^2\,{\rm log}|\lambda_i|^2.
\]
The coefficients \(\lambda_i\) specify the normalized GHZ state. This example demonstrates both the familiar two-party limit and the extra dependence on the number of parties. It also illustrates why a multipartite quantity can distinguish information that is lost when one examines only selected reduced-state spectra. The paper gives an explicit isospectral example to make that distinction concrete.
For holographic states, the same replica construction becomes a boundary condition for a gravitational path integral. Assuming the relevant replica symmetry extends into the bulk, the replicated geometry can be quotiented by that symmetry. Fixed loci become conical defects, represented in the calculation by cosmic branes. In the multipartite construction several such loci can meet, producing a connected web rather than a single separating surface.
The gravitational action near these defects determines the leading answer. The paper checks possible extra contributions at junctions by excising small tubular neighborhoods and examining the corner terms. In Einstein gravity, those junction contributions vanish as the neighborhood shrinks. Near \(n=1\), the brane tension vanishes, and the web can therefore be found as an area-minimizing probe configuration in the original geometry.
This gives the classical soap-film prescription:
\[
S^{(\mathtt{q})}=\frac{A(\mathcal{W})}{4G_N}.
\]
The web \(\mathcal{W}\) must end on the boundaries of the specified regions and contain subwebs homologous to each region. Together, these anchoring and homology conditions associate the bulk chambers with the specified boundary parties. The resulting geometry resembles a soap film attached to a wire frame, which motivates the name “soap-film prescription.”



Figure 2. Top view of the junction of tubular neighborhoods of three \(\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}\) sheets. (arXiv:2206.09723)

title: A New Multipartite Entanglement Measure and Its Holographic Dual
section: Quantum geometry and the replica construction
text:
Quantum geometry and the replica construction
The soap-film prescription extends the geometric dictionary of holography from a bipartition to a symmetric many-party observable. Its junctions describe a single bulk partition associated with all the boundary regions. In a three-dimensional spatial slice, minimizing the area gives the familiar local geometry of soap films: three sheets meet along a line at equal angles, and the junction lines can themselves meet at isolated points. The minimization determines both the shape of the sheets and their meeting conditions.
The replica construction supplies the link between this geometric problem and the boundary invariant. A replica-symmetric bulk saddle in Einstein gravity produces the classical area formula. The continuous brane tension then provides a manifest continuation of that saddle toward \(n=1\), where the branes become probes. This is the setting in which the multi-entropy is defined through analytic continuation; generalized GHZ states provide another explicitly computable family. The continuation connects integer-copy contractions to an entropy-like quantity that can be compared with a bulk area.
At the quantum level, fields in the chambers also share multipartite entanglement. The proposed quantum extremal soap-film prescription incorporates this contribution by extremizing
\[
\frac{A(\mathcal{W})}{4G_N}+S_{\rm bulk}^{(\mathtt{q})}(\mathcal{W}).
\]
The second term is the bulk multi-entropy for the chamber decomposition defined by the web. This conjectural extension gives quantum correlations a role in determining the location of the surface itself, in parallel with quantum extremal surfaces for ordinary entropy. The associated entropy includes the expectation value of the area operator and the renormalized bulk contribution.
A proposed covariant version replaces minimal webs on a fixed spatial slice with extremal webs, using a maximin construction to choose the appropriate configuration. The static, covariant, and quantum proposals organize multipartite entanglement around the same geometric ingredients: boundary regions, bulk chambers, and the surfaces joining them. Their shared structure motivates a broader study of replica invariants as probes of the way quantum states encode spacetime.

title: Monotonicity Conjecture for Multi-party Entanglement I
text:
Coarse graining a multipartite state
A multipartite quantum state can be viewed at different resolutions. Four laboratories may be treated separately, or two may be grouped into a single laboratory. The underlying state does not change, but the distinction between correlations inside a party and correlations between parties does. A measure intended to capture multipartite entanglement should respond meaningfully to this change of perspective. This paper investigates the proposal that a family of measures should not increase when parties are merged: monotonicity under coarse graining.
The proposal concerns pure states and a family called Rényi multi-entropies. It complements local-unitary invariance, symmetry between parties, and additivity for independent product states. The desired ordering for a general family of measures is:
\[
\displaystyle{\cal M}^{({\mathtt{q}})}(|\Psi\rangle)-{\cal M}^{({\mathtt{q}}-1)}(|\Psi_{[A_{\mathtt{a}}A_{\mathtt{b}}]}\rangle)\geq 0\qquad\quad\forall\,{\mathtt{a}},{\mathtt{b}}.
\]
The bracketed subscript means that two Hilbert-space factors are now regarded as one party. Repeated mergers generate many inequalities, organized by the partial order of partitions of the original parties. Thus the conjecture is a hierarchy rather than a single three-party comparison. An inequality for one merger can constrain every route through which a finely partitioned system is reduced to a coarser description.
Coarse graining changes which operations count as local: a joint unitary on the merged party can scramble degrees of freedom that previously belonged to separate laboratories. Local-unitary invariance makes the coarser measure insensitive to this scrambling. The proposed ordering therefore compares correlations resolved at two different scales within the same pure state. This gives a concrete counterpart to the familiar intuition that combining parties hides some of the multipartite structure.

title: Monotonicity Conjecture for Multi-party Entanglement I
section: Replica lattices and several routes to evidence
text:
Replica lattices and several routes to evidence
The construction begins with a polynomial local-unitary invariant: copies of the wavefunction and its complex conjugate are contracted with permutation-defined patterns. For Rényi multi-entropy the permutations are lattice translations, and the contraction can be drawn as a periodic lattice. Figure 1 shows a connected component of the three-party example. Its directions represent different parties, so identifying parties changes the contraction geometry in a controlled way.



Figure 1. A connected component of the invariant obtained by choosing three independent generators of \(\mathbb{Z}_{3}\times\mathbb{Z}_{3}\times\mathbb{Z}_{3}\) for the three party permutations. (arXiv:2308.16247)


The Rényi multi-entropy is a logarithm of that invariant with a normalization depending on the number of parties. It is defined by:
\[
\displaystyle S_{n}^{({\mathtt{q}})}:=\frac{1}{1-n}\frac{1}{n^{{\mathtt{q}}-2}}{\rm log}({\cal E}_{n}^{({\mathtt{q}})}).
\]
This normalization is necessary when comparing descriptions with different numbers of parties. It also makes the entropy additive for independent tensor-product states, since their polynomial invariants multiply. Where the logarithm is defined, the entropy ordering has an equivalent formulation directly in terms of polynomial invariants. This polynomial form is useful for analytic proofs and numerical tests:
\[
\displaystyle{S}_{n}^{({\mathtt{q}})}(|\psi\rangle)\geq{S}_{n}^{({\mathtt{q}}-1)}(|\psi_{[A_{\mathtt{a}}A_{\mathtt{b}}]}\rangle)\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad{\cal E}_{n}^{({\mathtt{q}})}(|\psi\rangle)\leq\Big({\cal E}_{n}^{({\mathtt{q}}-1)}(|\psi_{[A_{\mathtt{a}}A_{\mathtt{b}}]}\rangle)\Big)^{n}.
\]
Several complementary calculations then probe this assertion. Perturbation theory around factorized density matrices verifies it to second order, where the comparison reduces to controlled quadratic expressions. For classical probability distributions, regarded as diagonal density matrices of a purification, the proof uses inequalities between positive coefficients. Generalized three-party W states give another analytic test with genuinely quantum correlations. In that example the replica contraction can be reorganized as a lattice problem and related to a dimer model.



Figure 2. Resolution of the four-valent density matrix in the lattice representation of the W-state invariant. (arXiv:2308.16247)


The calculations are supplemented by numerical tests of randomly selected finite-dimensional states with several party numbers, dimensions, and replica indices. Agreement across these examples is evidence for the conjecture, while each analytic argument has its stated domain. The variety matters: diagonal states, small perturbations, W states, and random states probe different aspects of the same contraction inequality rather than repeating one special calculation.

title: Monotonicity Conjecture for Multi-party Entanglement I
text:
Holographic monotonicity and saturation
A holographic argument supplies a geometrical perspective at replica index two. Under the brane-web prescription, merging parties removes interfaces between the corresponding bulk chambers. The cone parameter on an interface is continuously reduced until that singular segment disappears. The gravitational action responds according to a Schläfli-type formula. The action derivative takes the form:
\[
\displaystyle\partial_{n}S({\widetilde{\cal B}}_{n}^{({\mathtt{2}})})=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\frac{1}{4G_{N}}A({\cal W}).
\]
Its positive-area right-hand side controls the direction of change. The method connects an information-theoretic inequality to the response of a hyperbolic cone geometry, provided the relevant saddle and continuation satisfy the geometric assumptions.
For a general multipartite state, this ordering is the monotonicity conjecture. The analytic proofs establish it for the stated classes, and the numerical tests explore systems with three, four, and five parties at several dimensions and replica indices. The polynomial formulation places these calculations in a common language: merging parties changes the contraction pattern, and the desired result compares the resulting homogeneous polynomials. Near a factorized state, the first-order terms saturate the comparison and the second-order terms determine the sign.
In the two-dimensional holographic setting at replica index two, the replica-symmetric cone-geometry prescription gives a direct realization of the merger operation. Each chamber touches a specified boundary region. The wall between two chambers disappears when its cone parameter reaches one, leaving precisely the coarser partition. Integrating the positive action derivative compares the two configurations. If the chambers already share no separating wall, the geometry remains unchanged and the coarse-graining inequality is saturated.
Saturation offers a way to identify which correlations a chosen merger removes. In the three-party examples, the discussion relates equality to factorization of the relevant reduced density matrix and to vanishing mutual information. In holography, equality can instead be read from the connectivity of the chamber decomposition. These complementary descriptions motivate multipartite versions of mutual information that diagnose correlations at different resolutions. They connect a proposed ordering of quantum states to a concrete question about which interfaces a gravitational geometry retains.

title: Multi-invariants and Bulk Replica Symmetry
text:
Multipartite invariants and replica symmetry
Entanglement between several parts of a quantum system contains information that cannot be captured by examining just one division into two parts. A natural starting point is to construct quantities unchanged by independent changes of basis in each part. This paper calls these quantities multi-invariants. It studies polynomial invariants obtained by contracting copies of a wavefunction with copies of its complex conjugate, with a separate contraction pattern for each party. Permutations record those patterns, turning a potentially complicated tensor expression into a precise combinatorial object.
The physical setting is the vacuum of a two-dimensional holographic conformal field theory: a theory with large central charge and a suitable gap that admits a semiclassical gravitational description. Dividing the spatial circle into party regions makes its vacuum a multipartite state. Each contraction becomes an instruction for gluing copies of the Euclidean path integral. The resulting replicated surface can have handles and branch points. Evaluating its partition function computes the invariant, with normalization removing the original state’s norm.
The central question is whether this complicated replicated problem has a simpler description using a single copy of the boundary. The normalized invariant removes its overall replica multiplicity:
\[
\displaystyle\tilde{\mathcal{E}}\equiv{\mathcal{E}}^{1/{n_{r}}},
\]
Here the replica number counts copies of the wavefunction. When a replica symmetry acts freely and transitively on the copies, quotienting the replicated boundary returns the original sphere. If the dominant gravitational filling also preserves that symmetry, its quotient supplies a bulk geometry with this single-copy boundary. The problem therefore joins two questions: how the contraction patterns generate replica symmetries, and how those symmetries extend from a replicated surface into its gravitational filling.



Figure 1. Quotienting hyperbolic space by different free normal subgroups gives intermediate handlebodies of different genera. Quotienting each handlebody by its replica symmetry gives the same final orbifold. (arXiv:2411.00935)

title: Multi-invariants and Bulk Replica Symmetry
section: From replicated surfaces to hyperbolic orbifolds
text:
From replicated surfaces to hyperbolic orbifolds
With an unbroken bulk replica symmetry, the invariant is determined by the difference between the orbifold action and the unreplicated action:
\[
\displaystyle\tilde{\mathcal{E}}=e^{-S_{\rm grav}[\hat{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{E}}]+S_{\rm grav}[{\mathcal{B}}]}.
\]
The quotient geometry generally contains conical singularities: lines around which a full circuit covers less angle than in smooth space. In three-dimensional Euclidean gravity these geometries can be described using discrete groups of hyperbolic isometries, called Kleinian groups. Their algebra records how the replicated boundary and its bulk filling fit together. Reflection symmetries extend the construction and connect it to Coxeter groups, which are generated by reflections satisfying pairwise relations.
Figure 1 captures a striking consequence. One Kleinian group can contain different free normal subgroups. Quotienting by one such subgroup first gives a handlebody, and a further finite quotient produces the final orbifold. Different choices can change the genus and the replica presentation while leaving that orbifold unchanged. Consequently, infinitely large families of normalized invariants agree on the holographic vacuum at the semiclassical level. The common orbifold action thus organizes observables with different replica numbers into equivalence families on this semiclassical holographic state.
The classification also has a local geometric face. Singular lines meet at junctions constrained by which finite groups can act around a point. The allowed three-line junctions are associated with four families:
\[
\displaystyle(m_{12},m_{23},m_{31})=\quad(2,2,n),\quad(2,3,3),\quad(2,3,4),\quad(2,3,5).
\]
The integers determine cone angles and therefore encode differing effective cosmic-brane tensions. Figure 2 displays the associated junctions. The possible local geometries are fixed by the spherical reflection groups, tying the branching pattern of a singular network to a finite set of algebraic data.



Figure 2. Trivalent singular loci associated with the Coxeter groups \((2,2,n)\), \((2,3,3)\), \((2,3,4)\), and \((2,3,5)\). An edge label \(n\) specifies a cone angle \(2\pi/n\); the replica symmetry groups are shown beside the junctions. (arXiv:2411.00935)


Combining groups along shared subgroups builds more extensive singular networks. This construction separates invariants that preserve bulk replica symmetry only in some configurations of boundary regions from those that do so for every configuration. Requiring preservation throughout the configuration space is highly restrictive: the resulting extended replica groups are finite Coxeter groups. Their defining presentation is:
\[
\langle r_{1},\cdots r_{{\mathtt{q}}}|(r_{i}r_{j})^{m_{ij}}=e\rangle,\quad m_{ii}=1,\quad m_{ij}=m_{ji}\geq 2
\]

title: Multi-invariants and Bulk Replica Symmetry
text:
Geometric classification and CFT checks
The classification associates each admissible contraction pattern with a family of symmetric gravitational fillings. As boundary regions move, the corresponding singular networks evolve, and competing fillings can exchange dominance. The group-theoretic construction identifies the patterns for which a replica-symmetric description persists throughout configuration space. It also produces relations among regulated gravitational actions: different replicated manifolds can yield the same action per replica when their fillings share a common quotient.
Direct CFT calculations test selected predictions independently of the bulk quotient construction. Twist operators impose the required permutation monodromies at the region endpoints. Covering maps lift these insertions to a smooth surface, and the accompanying Liouville action accounts for the change of metric. In the examples evaluated explicitly, this boundary calculation agrees with the gravitational orbifold result, connecting the same invariant to both a conformal mapping problem and a hyperbolic volume.
The saddle structure also includes examples with broken replica symmetry. For certain invariants, replica-symmetric solutions appear as subleading Euclidean wormholes with two boundary components, while a different filling dominates. Comparing their actions reveals how symmetry and topology organize the gravitational path integral. Within the vacuum of a two-dimensional holographic CFT, this supplies a geometric account of both the equivalence families of multi-invariants and the transitions among their bulk descriptions. The semiclassical theory thereby turns a large collection of tensor contractions into a tractable problem of discrete groups and hyperbolic geometry.

title: Phases of Supersymmetric Ground States in AdS₄
text:
Motivation and setup
Supersymmetry places a lower bound on the energy of a state with specified charges. States that saturate it are BPS states, the supersymmetric ground states in their charge sector. Black holes account for enormous numbers of such states, yet familiar regular BPS black holes do not exist at every allowed charge. This work asks what fills the rest of the phase diagram, and how these additional states affect the protected count called the superconformal index.
The setting is supergravity on \(AdS_4\times S^7\), restricted to four electric charges equal in pairs. There are consequently two independent electric charges, \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\), and one angular momentum, \(J\). The BPS energy bound is
\[
E\ell\geq J+2(Q_{1}\ell+Q_{2}\ell)~.
\]
Here \(\ell\) is the AdS radius. Saturating this linear inequality is necessary for supersymmetry, but a regular single black hole must also obey a nonlinear charge relation. After rescaling charges by the large-\(N\) parameter \(k=\ell^2/(2G)\), the paper uses densities \(q_1,q_2,j\), their sum \(q\), and difference \(\tilde q\). The nonlinear relation defines the “black hole sheet”:
\[
\displaystyle j=j_{c}(q,\tilde{q})=q\left(\sqrt{1+4\left(q^{2}-\tilde{q}^{2}\right)}-1\right)~.
\]
This sheet is a surface in a three-dimensional charge space. It does not fill the physical region. Its geometry therefore exposes the central puzzle: generic supersymmetric charge sectors cannot be described by an isolated member of the known black-hole family. The paper proposes that they instead contain a black-hole core accompanied by another component carrying the remaining charge.



Figure 1. The black hole sheet meets the \(j=0\) plane at \(q=|\tilde q|\) and shrinks inward as \(j\) increases. Light green is the translucent foreground; dark green shows the second branch where the sheet folds behind it. (arXiv:2510.16274)

title: Phases of Supersymmetric Ground States in AdS₄
text:
Construction and results
The construction assumes a two-component system whose energy and charges add at leading order. One component is a BPS black hole; the other is termed a gas. The gas carries macroscopic charge but negligible leading entropy, so the total entropy comes from the core. In the large-\(N\) thermodynamic description, these assumptions reduce the phase problem to a competition among possible core black holes. Grey-galaxy and dual-giant constructions motivate the two ways the additional component can carry charge.
Given total charges, the allowed cores lie on the black hole sheet and must leave nonnegative charges for the gas. The dominant candidate is found by maximizing the core entropy over that allowed set. On the sheet, the entropy density takes the simple form
\[
s_{BH}(j,q)=\pi\frac{j}{q}~.
\]
This constrained optimization produces distinct phases. On the overrotating side, called Region I, the entropy is greatest when the core retains all electric charge and the gas carries the excess angular momentum. This has the character of a grey galaxy, with angular momentum stored far from the central black hole.
On the overcharged side, Region II, the optimum places all angular momentum in the core while the gas carries electric charge. There are two cases. In Region IIa the core can reach equal electric charges, and the gas absorbs the charge imbalance. In Region IIb the positivity constraints prevent that equal-charge core; the optimum instead has gas carrying only one of the two electric charges. These charged configurations are motivated by dual giant gravitons, with an \(M2\)-brane interpretation in this compactification.
The superconformal index introduces another optimization. Because its chemical potentials obey a supersymmetric constraint, it resolves combinations of charges rather than all three charges independently. In the paper’s density variables, an index line has fixed \(\zeta=q+j\) and \(\tilde\zeta=\tilde q\). Each physical line intersects the black hole sheet once, but this intersection need not supply its largest entropy.
Assuming that cancellations in the signed index do not remove the leading entropy maximum, the paper compares configurations along each line. For nonnegative \(\tilde\zeta\), the resulting prediction is
\[
s_{\mathcal{I}}(\zeta,\tilde{\zeta})=\begin{cases}s_{X}(\zeta,\tilde{\zeta})&,~~{\rm if~~}\tilde{\zeta}\leq\frac{1}{2}\\
s_{max}(\zeta,\tilde{\zeta})&,~~{\rm if~~}\tilde{\zeta}>\frac{1}{2}\end{cases}
\]
The quantity \(s_X\) is the entropy of the pure black hole at the intersection; \(s_{max}\) is the larger two-component maximum. Exchanging the electric charges extends the transition to negative \(\tilde\zeta\). Thus sufficiently unequal charges change the phase dominating the predicted index.

title: Phases of Supersymmetric Ground States in AdS₄
text:
Phase transitions in the index



Figure 2. The microcanonical index phase diagram in the physical region \(|\tilde\zeta|\leq\zeta\). Grey is the pure BPS black-hole phase and blue is the two-component phase, connected by second-order transitions at \(|\tilde\zeta|=1/2\). (arXiv:2510.16274)


The ground-state and index phase diagrams describe different ensembles. Fixing all conserved charges selects the best core compatible with one point in charge space. Fixing the index charges instead selects an entire line, along which angular momentum and the sum of electric charges vary together. The maximal entropy along this line determines the index prediction under the unobstructed saddle assumption. A two-component configuration can supply that maximum even though the line also contains a pure black hole.
When the electric charges are comparable, the entropy increases along the grey-galaxy segment toward the pure black hole and then decreases along the overcharged segment. The black-hole intersection is consequently the dominant point. For a sufficiently large charge difference, an additional maximum appears in the two-component part of the line. This maximum overtakes the pure black hole at \(|\tilde\zeta|=1/2\), producing the second-order transition. At the positive boundary, the two entropy branches both equal \(\pi(-1+\sqrt{2\zeta})\). Exchanging the two electric charges gives the corresponding negative boundary.
Complex Euclidean BPS black holes provide a complementary description through chemical potentials conjugate to the conserved charges. A convergent interpretation of the index requires the real parts of the relevant potentials to suppress towers of charged states. The onset of instability in this description coincides with the predicted transition to the two-component phase. The geometry and the statistical ensemble therefore identify the same threshold through different calculations.
The Kontsevich–Segal–Witten condition tests positivity of auxiliary-field kinetic terms on the complex metric. In this \(AdS_4\) charge sector it remains satisfied across the statistical instability, distinguishing geometric allowability from thermodynamic dominance. Together, these results give a coherent organization of the leading large-\(N\) ground states: entropy is stored in a black-hole core, charge can also reside in an accompanying component, and the index selects among these configurations according to the charge combinations it resolves.
